newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks brace for Fed, earnings.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks brace for Fed, earnings.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market is bracing itself for the outcome of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-setting meeting scheduled for Tuesday and a series of domestic corporate results this coming week, brokers said.
They said U.S. stocks could receive a boost if the Fed leaves rates unchanged. That, in turn, would support the Tokyo market.
But on Friday U.S. stocks and bonds fell sharply as robust economic news fanned fears that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 138.88 points, or 1.89 percent, to 7,194.67.
The interest rate jitters started boiling after the U.S. government reported housing starts rose by a stronger-than-expected 2.6 percent in April.
On Friday, the market's benchmark Nikkei 225 average finished at 20,324.73, up 521.95 points from May 9.
Investors will also be keeping an eye on Japanese economic indicators, such as trade balance figures for January, due on Monday, and industrial production for March, due on Tuesday.
This week is also the peak period for companies issuing earnings results, including city banks, smaller local banks and construction firms.

"The focus is whether the earnings reports reignite worries over the Japanese financial system. If the market passes the earnings without big problems, stocks would power higher again," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.

The market will also pay close attention to recent volatile currency movements. But unless the dollar drops far below 115 yen, where many Japanese firms set their internal dollar/yen rate, the yen's strength alone was not likely to pull the Nikkei lower, brokers said.
"The market is likely to keep a firm tone, as blue-chip multinationals did not fall much despite the yen's rise," said a broker at a "Big Four" securities house.
Some also said the market was hypersensitive about the yen's rally.

"A brief slide in the dollar below 115 yen may water down investors' interest in export-driven issues, but what is more important is these exporters' profitability for the whole year," said Shinichi Ichikawa, strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities.
"If the shares, such as in the high-tech sector, fall, it should be a good chance for bargain-hunting," he said.
On Friday, issues driven by domestic demand, such as Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), attracted investors due to the yen's recent firmness against the dollar.
"Since the yen's surge, investors have kept from buying exporters actively, and NTT attracted investors as one of the possible leading issues in the future," Ishijima said.
NTT also attracted interest because it will be included in the Morgan Stanley Capital International index, brokers said.
The shares closed 40,000 yen higher at 1.07 million yen, a fresh high for this calendar year.
